primary_excavation_witness.author: J. E. Quibell
primary_excavation_witness.title: Note on a tomb found at Tell er Roba
primary_excavation_witness.publication: Annales du Service des Antiquites de l'Egypte 3
primary_excavation_witness.site: Tell er Roba / Tell el-Rub'a, Mendes
primary_excavation_witness.burial_context: Gold objects were found on the body below the slab; more than 350 faience ushabtis and probably other unknown objects had already been removed by workmen before the inspector intervened.
primary_excavation_witness.exact_object_class_statement: Quibell reports that gold foil was used to make rough sheaths covering the fingers, toes and phallus.

material_geometry.minimum_geometry: A thin gold covering was fitted around/on the phallus of the mummy.
not_resolved: whether the phallus sheath had a closed or open distal end
whether it was cylindrical, conical, anatomically modelled, or only folded foil
whether it was detachable during ritual use

site_and_person_chain.role: priest whose titles associate him with the cult of Banebdjedet
site_and_person_chain.modern_museum_cross_reference: The Metropolitan Museum of Art states that the mummy in the chamber was adorned with gold-leaf trappings and refers to Cairo CG 53465-53469.

inventory_completeness.primary_warning: Quibell explicitly states that the workmen had already removed more than 350 ushabtis and probably other objects of which the excavators knew nothing.
inventory_completeness.implication: Absence of another target object from Quibell's recovered list cannot prove that such an object never existed in the tomb.

relation_to_current_mendes_hypotheses.IMPORTANT_RESULT: The reverse/Tenet possibility that a metallic sheath can fit around a male genital organ is now archaeologically real in the precise Mendes site context, but the attested object is a human funerary mummy accessory rather than the textual metal kꜣ.t.

sources.use: site context, incomplete recovery, gold-on-body context, gold phallus sheath object-class
